Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) — Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have resigned as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to leave office.

Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address on Sunday. His successor, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, will be sworn in as South Africa’s president on Thursday.

Mbeki’s announcement prompted several Cabinet members to threaten to follow suit, although the outgoing president urged them to remain in office, government sources said.

The resignations—including those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will take effect on Thursday, when Mbeki steps down, according to a government statement.

“All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them,” the statement said.

Manuel’s assistant told CNN that the finance minister would be willing to serve in the new government if needed. Three deputy ministers have also tendered their resignations, according to a government statement.

A spokesman for South Africa’s ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that the party had selected Motlanthe to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will remain in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win.

Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge dismissed the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma, Mbeki’s political archrival. The judge declared the case invalid and accused Mbeki’s government of political interference.

Mbeki, who has served as South Africa’s president for nearly 10 years, highlighted some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation during Sunday’s televised address.

Watch the significance of Mbeki “falling on the sword” »

“I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all,” Mbeki said.

Under his leadership, South Africa experienced the longest period of sustained economic growth in its history and reached out to indigent people in an unprecedented way, Mbeki said.

He acknowledged that the country would continue to face economic, corruption and crime-related challenges. He also expressed confidence in the country’s next leader without identifying who that person would be.

Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress—a party Mbeki has been involved with since his teenage years—announced Saturday that the ANC had asked Mbeki to leave office before the end of his term. Mbeki agreed to do so, Mantashe said.

Mantashe said the ANC had made the decision “for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country” and so the ANC movement could remain “stable and unified.”

The case against Zuma, who replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year, was dismissed in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority later recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson made no ruling on Zuma’s guilt or innocence, and Zuma could be charged again.

Political observers doubted that this would happen because of Zuma’s popularity, particularly among the Communist Party and trade unions.

Zuma has denied the charges, saying the case was politically motivated and had harmed his chances of becoming the ANC’s presidential nominee.

If convicted of accepting bribes from a company that secured a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, Zuma could have faced at least 15 years in prison. He also faced charges related to an allegedly corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma’s political influence to benefit his businesses.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa’s president in June 1999. Critics alleged that he had pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma.

Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe’s political rivals, who signed the deal on Monday in an effort to put their violent past behind them and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March.

Under the agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

Mbeki publicly confirmed in a televised speech on Sunday that he would step down. Kgalema Motlanthe, deputy president of the African National Congress, is expected to replace him and will be inaugurated as national president on Thursday.

Following Mbeki’s announcement, several Cabinet members threatened to resign as well, although government sources said the departing president encouraged them to remain in their posts. According to an official statement, the resignations—including those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will become effective Thursday, when Mbeki leaves office.

The government said every resigning minister had indicated a willingness to help the new administration with the transition and to provide any additional support requested. Manuel’s assistant told CNN that the finance minister would also be prepared to serve under the incoming government if called upon. Three deputy ministers have tendered their resignations as well.

A representative of the governing ANC confirmed that the party selected Motlanthe to succeed Mbeki. He is due to serve until elections in the spring of the following year, when ANC President Jacob Zuma is broadly expected to win.

The ANC called on Mbeki to resign earlier in the month after a judge dismissed corruption, fraud and racketeering charges against Zuma, Mbeki’s principal political rival. The judge found the prosecution invalid and alleged that Mbeki’s administration had interfered for political reasons.

During Sunday’s formal televised resignation announcement, Mbeki, who had led South Africa for almost a decade, reviewed some of the accomplishments of his presidency. His decision was portrayed as politically “falling on the sword.”

Mbeki said he was leaving office with the knowledge that many South African men and women had worked toward improving life for everyone. He credited his administration with overseeing the longest uninterrupted period of economic expansion in the country’s history and with providing unprecedented assistance to impoverished citizens.

At the same time, he acknowledged that South Africa continued to face future difficulties involving the economy, corruption and crime. Without identifying his successor, Mbeki also expressed confidence in whoever would next lead the country.

ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe announced on Saturday that the organization—of which Mbeki had been a member since his teenage years—had requested that he leave office before completing his term. Mbeki accepted the request, Mantashe said.

According to Mantashe, the ANC acted in the interests of South Africans, with the goal of preserving national stability and keeping the party movement united and secure.

The case against Zuma, who replaced Mbeki as ANC president the previous year, was initially dismissed in September 2006. The National Prosecuting Authority later filed the charges again. Judge Chris Nicholson did not determine whether Zuma was guilty or innocent, meaning prosecutors could still recharge him.

Political analysts considered another prosecution unlikely because Zuma enjoyed strong support, especially from labor unions and the Communist Party. Zuma denied the allegations, arguing that the case was driven by politics and had damaged his prospects of becoming the ANC’s presidential candidate.

A conviction for accepting bribes from a company awarded a contract in a multibillion-dollar weapons deal could have resulted in a prison term of at least 15 years. Zuma was also accused of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik. Shaik was serving a 15-year sentence for seeking bribes on Zuma’s behalf and exploiting Zuma’s political influence to advance his own business interests.

Mbeki, 66, became South African president in June 1999, succeeding Nelson Mandela. His opponents alleged that he had pressed for the corruption prosecution of Zuma.

More recently, Mbeki mediated a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe’s rival political factions. The deal, signed on Monday, was intended to move beyond the country’s violent past and resolve the paralysis that followed disputed national elections in March.

Under that arrangement, longtime Zimbabwean ruler Robert Mugabe retained the presidency, while his enduring opponent, Morgan Tsvangirai, became prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

The move briefly caused financial-market concern, especially over Manuel, but some resigning ministers indicated they were willing to serve under the next president.

He appointed a new Cabinet, retained or reappointed several experienced ministers—including Trevor Manuel—and named Baleka Mbete deputy president. Motlanthe’s main role was to provide stability and lead the country until the 2009 general election.
- **Jacob Zuma**, who had defeated Mbeki for the ANC presidency in December 2007, remained the ANC’s political leader but did not immediately become national president. Motlanthe effectively served as a caretaker while Zuma prepared to lead the ANC into the 2009 election.
- After the ANC won that election, Parliament elected **Zuma president in May 2009**, succeeding Motlanthe.

Thus, Mbeki’s departure produced a partial Cabinet exodus, a short Motlanthe transitional presidency, and ultimately Zuma’s rise to the presidency.

# Mbeki resigns as South African ministers follow amid ANC power struggle

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa —** South African President Thabo Mbeki resigned in September 2008 after the governing African National Congress ordered him to step down, triggering the departure of several senior ministers and deepening the country’s most serious political crisis since the end of apartheid.

Eleven Cabinet members, including Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, submitted their resignations, along with several deputy ministers. Manuel later said he was willing to serve in the next government, helping calm financial markets concerned about the continuity of South Africa’s economic policy.

Mbeki agreed to leave office after the ANC’s National Executive Committee “recalled” him, effectively withdrawing the party’s mandate for him to govern. Parliament subsequently elected ANC deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe as interim president until national elections in 2009.

The upheaval exposed a bitter division inside the ANC between supporters of Mbeki and allies of Jacob Zuma, who had defeated Mbeki for the party leadership at its December 2007 conference in Polokwane.

## Court ruling accelerates Mbeki’s fall

The immediate catalyst was a court ruling that set aside corruption charges against Zuma on procedural grounds. Judge Chris Nicholson suggested there may have been political interference in the decision to prosecute Zuma and said the timing of the case could support an inference that Mbeki’s government had sought to undermine a political rival.

Mbeki denied interfering with prosecutors and asked South Africa’s Constitutional Court to challenge findings he said had damaged his reputation without giving him an opportunity to respond.

Nicholson’s allegations intensified pressure from Zuma’s supporters, who had long claimed the prosecution was politically motivated. The ANC leadership then demanded Mbeki’s resignation, roughly seven months before his second presidential term was due to end.

The political-interference findings were later overturned on appeal, with a higher court saying Nicholson had gone beyond the issues he was required to decide.

## The corruption case against Zuma

The case centered on South Africa’s multibillion-dollar arms procurement program of the late 1990s.

Prosecutors alleged that Zuma had received improper financial benefits from his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, and that Shaik had sought an annual payment for Zuma from French arms company Thint, formerly known as Thomson-CSF. The alleged payment was intended to secure Zuma’s protection from investigations connected to the arms deal, prosecutors said.

Zuma denied wrongdoing and said the charges were part of a campaign to block his rise to the presidency.

Shaik was convicted in 2005 of fraud and corruption. During that trial, a judge described the relationship between Shaik and Zuma as “generally corrupt.” Mbeki then dismissed Zuma as South Africa’s deputy president, setting off the political confrontation that eventually divided the ANC.

Charges against Zuma were repeatedly filed, withdrawn and reinstated as prosecutors and defense lawyers fought over procedure and evidence. In April 2009, shortly before the national election, prosecutors dropped the case after recordings appeared to show officials discussing the timing of charges for political reasons. That decision would itself later face years of legal challenges.

## A divided liberation movement

Mbeki’s removal marked a dramatic reversal for a leader who had succeeded Nelson Mandela and presided over years of economic growth. But critics accused his administration of being distant, centralized and insufficiently responsive to poverty, unemployment and the HIV/AIDS crisis.

Zuma drew support from trade unions, the South African Communist Party, ANC youth activists and members who believed Mbeki had concentrated too much power in the presidency.

The Cabinet resignations raised fears of a broader government collapse, but many officials emphasized that the transition would be orderly. Motlanthe’s appointment was intended to provide stability while Zuma prepared to lead the ANC into the 2009 election.

The crisis ultimately showed that the ANC’s internal leadership contest had moved beyond party structures and into the institutions of the state—splitting former allies and ending Mbeki’s presidency before voters went to the polls.

# South Africa Faces Cabinet Upheaval as Mbeki Prepares to Leave Office

**CAPE TOWN, South Africa, Sept. 23, 2008** — South Africa’s political crisis deepened Tuesday as President Thabo Mbeki prepared to leave office and more than a dozen members of his government, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defence Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, submitted their resignations.

The departures followed the governing African National Congress’s decision at the weekend to “recall” Mr. Mbeki, effectively ordering him to step down before the end of his second term next year. Parliament is expected to accept his resignation and elect ANC deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe as the country’s interim president. Mr. Motlanthe is scheduled to be sworn in on Thursday.

The wave of resignations raised fears that the removal of Mr. Mbeki could disrupt the government and unsettle an economy already under pressure from high inflation, slowing growth and global financial turmoil. The rand fell sharply after news that Mr. Manuel, the long-serving finance minister and one of South Africa’s most internationally respected officials, had resigned.

Government officials moved quickly to limit the damage, stressing that the resignations were constitutionally required or offered as a matter of political principle and did not necessarily mean all the ministers would refuse to serve under the next president. Mr. Manuel indicated that he would be willing to remain in office if asked by the incoming administration.

The presidency said the resignations would take effect at the same time as Mr. Mbeki’s departure. Other officials leaving included Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and several ministers and deputy ministers associated with the outgoing president.

Mr. Lekota’s resignation carried particular political significance. A former ANC national chairman and a veteran of the anti-apartheid struggle, he had become an outspoken critic of the party leadership’s treatment of Mr. Mbeki. His departure highlighted widening divisions between supporters of the outgoing president and the ANC faction aligned with Jacob Zuma.

## Motlanthe to Take Over

Mr. Motlanthe, a former trade unionist and one-time ANC secretary-general, entered Parliament only months ago and was appointed to the cabinet in July. He is widely regarded as a conciliatory figure capable of managing the transition until national elections, expected in 2009.

Under South Africa’s Constitution, Parliament elects the president. Because the ANC holds a commanding legislative majority, Mr. Motlanthe’s election is considered virtually certain.

He is expected to serve as a caretaker rather than as a rival to Mr. Zuma, the ANC president and the party’s presumed candidate to lead the country after the election. Mr. Zuma does not currently sit in Parliament, making Mr. Motlanthe the more practical choice to complete the remainder of Mr. Mbeki’s term.

The ANC has insisted that the transition will be orderly and that government policy will remain stable. But the number and seniority of those resigning have intensified questions about whether the party can contain its internal conflict.

## Mbeki Recalled After Zuma Court Ruling

The crisis was triggered by a High Court ruling earlier this month that set aside corruption-related charges against Mr. Zuma on procedural grounds.

Judge Chris Nicholson ruled that prosecutors had failed to give Mr. Zuma an opportunity to make representations before deciding to charge him again. The judge also suggested that there had been political interference in the prosecution, including possible involvement by senior officials in Mr. Mbeki’s administration.

The ruling did not determine Mr. Zuma’s guilt or innocence, and prosecutors have disputed its broader political findings. Nevertheless, Mr. Mbeki’s opponents within the ANC seized on the judgment as evidence that state institutions had been used to damage Mr. Zuma’s political career.

Mr. Mbeki has strongly denied interfering in the prosecution.

Mr. Zuma was dismissed as deputy president of South Africa in 2005 after his financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption and fraud. The case exposed a bitter struggle inside the ANC. Although Mr. Zuma later faced charges including corruption, fraud, money laundering and racketeering, he retained strong support among trade unions, the South African Communist Party, the ANC Youth League and many rank-and-file party members.

That coalition helped Mr. Zuma defeat Mr. Mbeki for the ANC presidency at the party’s conference in Polokwane in December 2007. Since then, the country has been governed under an uneasy arrangement in which Mr. Mbeki remained national president while Mr. Zuma controlled the governing party.

The Nicholson judgment brought that rivalry to a head. After meeting over the weekend, the ANC’s national executive committee instructed Mr. Mbeki to resign. He agreed, saying in a televised address that he accepted the decision despite rejecting allegations that he had abused his office.

## Economic Anxiety

Mr. Manuel’s resignation was the most immediate concern for investors. Finance minister since 1996, he has overseen a period of fiscal discipline and economic expansion, building credibility for post-apartheid South Africa in international markets.

The government sought to reassure businesses that the Treasury would continue functioning and that the country’s economic framework would not change abruptly. ANC officials said Mr. Manuel remained an important national asset, while his willingness to serve under Mr. Motlanthe eased some fears of a prolonged vacancy.

Even so, the episode showed how quickly the political struggle could spill into the economy. South Africa is confronting electricity shortages, high food and fuel prices, unemployment and widening public frustration over inequality and poor services.

Mr. Zuma’s allies have demanded greater attention to poverty and redistribution, but they have also repeatedly said that an ANC government under new leadership will not abandon macroeconomic stability.

## Zimbabwe Mediation in Question

Mr. Mbeki’s departure also created uncertainty over South Africa’s role in Zimbabwe, where he has served as the chief regional mediator between President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai.

Only days before the ANC moved against him, Mr. Mbeki had helped broker a power-sharing agreement intended to end Zimbabwe’s political deadlock. The accord followed disputed elections, months of violence and the collapse of the Zimbabwean economy.

Under the agreement, Mr. Mugabe was to remain president while Mr. Tsvangirai became prime minister. But the deal left key questions unresolved, including control of important ministries and the division of executive authority.

Mr. Mbeki’s policy of “quiet diplomacy” toward Zimbabwe has long been controversial. Critics accused him of failing to confront Mr. Mugabe over political repression and election abuses. Mr. Mbeki maintained that patient negotiation, rather than public condemnation, offered the best chance of preventing further instability.

Regional leaders may ask him to continue mediating in a personal capacity after he leaves office. His removal, however, could complicate implementation of the fragile agreement at a moment when Zimbabwe’s rival parties remain deeply divided.

## A Historic but Bitter Exit

Mr. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999 and won a second term in 2004. His administration presided over sustained economic growth and an expansion of South Africa’s influence across the continent. But his legacy has been damaged by criticism of his approach to HIV/AIDS, his handling of Zimbabwe and accusations that power became too concentrated in the presidency.

His forced departure marks the first time since the end of apartheid that the ANC has removed a sitting national president.

For the party that has governed South Africa since the first democratic election in 1994, the immediate challenge is to demonstrate unity while managing a transfer of power born from an exceptionally bitter internal contest.

Mr. Motlanthe’s expected swearing-in may settle the constitutional question of who governs the country. It is less likely to end the struggle over who controls the ANC — or the debate over the political and economic direction South Africa will take under Mr. Zuma’s ascendant leadership.
